notes.rule:
**Sono** says who you are, and **sei** says who someone you know well is. Both are forms of **essere**, to be.

Italian usually leaves out **io** and **tu**, because the verb already shows who is meant: **Sono Tom.**

Every noun is masculine or feminine. **Un** goes with a masculine noun (**un uomo**, **un ragazzo**), **una** with a feminine one (**una donna**, **una ragazza**).

To say not, put **non** before the verb: **Non sono Tom.**

A question keeps the same word order; only the voice rises: **Sei Tom?**

Three phrases to keep a conversation going.
**Non capisco** means I don't understand.
**Più lentamente**, or **più piano**, asks for slower speech.
**Ripeti** asks a friend to say it again, and **ripeta** asks politely.

**Parla** is for someone you call **tu** and **parli** for someone you call **Lei**. **Per favore** makes each one polite.

The word for the changes with the noun:
**il** before a masculine noun (**il libro**, **il dottore**)
**la** before a feminine one (**la casa**, **la donna**)
**l'** before any noun that starts with a vowel (**l'uomo**)

**Lui** is he and **lei** is she. **È**, with its accent, means is; **e** without one means and.

**Questo** and **questa** mean this: **questo** with a masculine noun, **questa** with a feminine one.

An adjective in **-o** changes to **-a** with a feminine noun (**piccolo**, **piccola**). One in **-e** stays the same (**grande**, **forte**).

Italian has two words for you. **Tu** is for a friend, a child or family. **Lei**, the same word as she, is the polite you for an adult you don't know well. It takes the verb form used for he and she.

To ask how someone is, Italian uses **stare**, not **essere**:
**Come stai?** (to a friend)
**Come sta?** (politely)
**Sto bene** (the answer)

**Scusa** is sorry to a friend, **scusi** the polite form. **Prego** answers **grazie**.

A verb changes its ending with the person: **mangio** is I eat, **mangi** you eat, **mangia** he or she eats. **Bevo**, **bevi**, **beve** work the same way for drinking.

To say what you like, Italian says it pleases me: **Mi piace il tè**. **Ti piace il tè?** asks a friend.

Food you like in general takes **il**, **la** or **l'**: **Mi piace il pane.**

**Avere** means to have: **ho** is I have, **hai** you have, **ha** he or she has. The **h** is never pronounced.

**Non** goes before the verb: **Non ho un cane.**
A question keeps the same words: **Hai un cane?**

Two questions for words you don't know.

**Come si dice…?** asks how something is said: **Come si dice questo in italiano?**

**Cosa significa…?** and **Cosa vuol dire…?** both ask what a word means.

**Che**, **cosa** and **che cosa** all mean what, and any of the three can start the question.

For more than one, a masculine noun in **-o** changes to **-i** (**libro**, **libri**) and a feminine noun in **-a** changes to **-e** (**mela**, **mele**). A few are irregular: **uomo** becomes **uomini**.

The word for the changes too:
**i** for most masculine plurals (**i libri**)
**gli** before a vowel (**gli uomini**, **gli amici**)
**le** for feminine plurals (**le mele**)

**Noi siamo** is we are, **voi siete** is you are when speaking to several people, and **loro sono** is they are. **Abbiamo**, **avete** and **hanno** are the same three forms of **avere**.

An adjective agrees with its noun: **buono**, **nuovo**, **vecchio** and **bello** with a masculine noun, **buona**, **nuova**, **vecchia** and **bella** with a feminine one. **Giovane** doesn't change.

Most adjectives come after the noun (**una macchina vecchia**), though a few common ones can come before it.

**Molto** before an adjective means very; after a verb it means a lot. **Anche** means also and comes before the word it adds.

**Mi piace** can take a verb as well as a noun: **Mi piace nuotare** means I like swimming. The verb stays in its dictionary form, ending in **-are** or **-ere**: **ballare**, **cantare**, **nuotare**, **leggere**.

With a person the ending changes:
**canto** is I sing and **canta** he or she sings
**leggo** is I read and **legge** he or she reads

**C'è** means there is, for one thing. **Ci sono** means there are, for more than one. Both can ask a question as they are: **C'è un cane qui?**

**In** says where, with no word for the: **in cucina**, **in bagno**, **in giardino**.
**Sul** means on the: **sul tavolo**, **sul letto**.

**Qui** is here and **lì** is there.

Some feelings use **essere** with an adjective, which agrees with the person. A man says **Sono stanco**, a woman **Sono stanca**. **Malato** and **malata** work the same way, while **felice** and **triste** don't change.

Others use **avere** with a noun, where English says to be:
**Ho fame** (I'm hungry)
**Ho sete** (I'm thirsty)
**Ho sonno** (I'm sleepy)
**Ho paura** (I'm afraid)
**Ho freddo** (I'm cold)
**Ho caldo** (I'm hot)

When the word won't come, say so and describe the thing.

**Cerco la parola** means I'm looking for the word.
**È una cosa per…** means it's a thing for…, followed by a verb: **È una cosa per leggere.**
**Come si chiama?** asks what something is called.
**Non lo so** means I don't know; **lo** stands for it.

**Sai** with a verb asks whether someone knows how: **Sai nuotare?**

My, your and his or her agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: **mio**, **tuo** and **suo** with a masculine noun, **mia**, **tua** and **sua** with a feminine one, **miei** and **mie** for the plurals. **Suo** and **sua** mean his, her or the polite your.

Italian puts the before them: **la mia casa**, **il mio libro**, **i miei amici**. One family member is the exception: **mio padre**, **mia madre**, with no the.

**Di** shows whose something is: **la casa di mia madre**.

Question words come first: **chi** (who), **cosa**, **che** or **che cosa** (what), **dove** (where), **quando** (when), **perché** (why), **quale** (which).

**Dove** and **è** join into **dov'è**, where is.

**Perché** also means because, so it starts the answer too:
**Perché sei triste?** **Perché sono stanco.**

**Dov'è…?** finds a place: **Dov'è la stazione?**

**In** says how you travel, with no word for the: **in treno**, **in autobus**, **in bicicletta**.

**Con** means with: **Sono con Tom.**
**Sul treno** means on the train.

The numbers from one to ten don't change with the noun, except **uno**, which becomes **un** or **una** before one. **Sei**, six, is spelled like **sei**, you are.

How many is **quanti** with a masculine plural (**quanti libri**) and **quante** with a feminine one (**quante mele**).

A color comes after its noun and agrees with it: **rosso**, **nero**, **bianco** and **giallo** with a masculine noun, **rossa**, **nera**, **bianca** and **gialla** with a feminine one. **Verde** stays the same for both, and **blu** never changes at all.

**Che colore è?** asks what color something is.

**Oggi** is today, **domani** tomorrow and **adesso** now. The days of the week have no capital letter.

**Che giorno è oggi?** asks the day.
**Che ora è?** asks the time. **Ora** means hour or time here.

**Andare**, to go, is irregular: **vado** is I go, **vai** you go, **va** he or she goes.

**A** means to or at: **a scuola**, with no word for the.
Before a masculine noun **a** and **il** join into **al** (**al parco**, **al ristorante**).
Before a feminine one **a** and **la** join into **alla** (**alla stazione**).

To describe someone, Italian uses **avere** with the:
**Ha i capelli lunghi** (she has long hair)
**Ho gli occhi azzurri** (I have blue eyes)

The adjective comes after the noun and agrees with it, so plural **capelli** and **occhi** take **lunghi** and **azzurri**. **Alto** describes a man and **alta** a woman.

**A piedi** means on foot.

To ask a friend's name, say **Come ti chiami?**
To ask politely, to someone you don't know, say **Come si chiama?**

That is **Lei**, the polite you. It is the same word as **lei** (she) and takes the same verb form, so **si chiama** means both her name is and your name is.

Answer with **Mi chiamo …** (my name is …).
**Piacere!** means pleased to meet you.
**Ti presento …** (**Le presento …**, politely) introduces someone.

**Potere** means can: **posso**, **puoi**, **può**. The verb after it stays in the infinitive:
**Posso chiedere?** (may I ask?)
**Puoi scrivere?** (can you write?)

To ask how a word is spelled, say **Come si scrive?**

Numbers from 11 to 20: **undici**, **dodici**, **tredici**, **quattordici**, **quindici**, **sedici**, **diciassette**, **diciotto**, **diciannove**, **venti**.

**Sei** is six, and also you are: the sentence makes it clear.

Phone numbers are said in pairs or one digit at a time, with **zero** for 0.

Italian uses **avere** for age: **Ho vent'anni** (I am twenty, literally I have twenty years). To ask, say **Quanti anni hai?**

**Sono nato** (a man) and **sono nata** (a woman) mean I was born.
**Buon compleanno!** is happy birthday.

Ways to check a number or ask for time:
**Un momento** (one moment)
**Aspetta** (wait)
**È giusto?** (is that right?)
**Certo!** (of course!)

**Giusto?** at the end of a sentence asks for a yes, like right? in English.

The tens are **trenta**, **quaranta**, **cinquanta**, **sessanta**, **settanta**, **ottanta**, **novanta**, then **cento** (100) and **mille** (1,000).

In between, the tens and units join into one word: **trentadue**, **quarantacinque**.

Before **uno** and **otto** the tens drop their last vowel: **ventuno**, **trentotto**.

**Abitare** and **vivere** both mean to live. **Abito**, **abiti**, **abita** follow the **-are** pattern, **vivo**, **vivi**, **vive** the **-ere** one.

Use **a** before a town and **in** before a country or a part of town: **Abito a Roma**, **vivo in Italia**, **abito in centro**.

**Vicino a** means near, **lontano** far.

Nationalities agree with the person: **italiano** for a man, **italiana** for a woman. **Francese** is the same for both.

Languages take no capital letter and usually the article: **il francese**, **l'inglese**, though **parlo francese** is fine.

**Parlare** follows the **-are** pattern: **parlo**, **parli**, **parla**.

**Volere** means to want: **voglio**, **vuoi**. **Vorrei** (I would like) is the polite way to ask for something in a shop.

**Dovere** means must: **devo**, **deve**.
**Ho bisogno di …** means I need ….

After a quantity, use **di**: **un chilo di mele**.

To show you've understood:
**D'accordo** (agreed, OK)
**Chiaro** (clear)
**Ho capito** (I've understood)
**Esatto** (exactly)

**Vero?** at the end of a sentence asks for a yes: **Sei d'accordo, vero?**

**Cioè** means that is, to make something clearer.

**Quanto costa?** asks the price of one thing. **Quanto costano?** asks the price of more than one: **costano** agrees with a plural.

**Costa due euro**: **euro** never changes in the plural.

**Caro** is expensive and **economico** cheap. **Il conto** is the bill.

After a container or an amount, use **di**: **una bottiglia di latte**, **un pacchetto di biscotti**, **un po' di pane**.

**Troppo** is too much, **poco** little, **abbastanza** enough.

**Quello** and **quella** mean that (masculine and feminine). **Ogni** (every) never changes: **ogni giorno**.

**Portare** is to wear (and also to bring): **porto**, **porti**.

**Gli occhiali** (glasses) and **i pantaloni** (trousers) are always plural.

Colors agree with the noun when they end in **-o**: **una gonna rossa**. But **blu** never changes.

**Studiare** follows the **-are** pattern: **studio**, **studi**, **studia**. **Imparare** means to learn.

**Una domanda** is a question and **una risposta** an answer. **Per esempio** means for example.

Adjectives agree with the person: **basso** for a man, **bassa** for a woman; **biondo**, **bionda**; **magro**, **magra**. Adjectives in **-e** are the same for both: **intelligente**.

**Lo stesso** means the same.

Adjectives in **-o** change for a woman and in the plural (**aperto**, **aperta**). Adjectives in **-e** are the same for both genders: **facile**, **difficile**, **importante**, **interessante**.

**È facile** means it's easy, **È importante** it's important.

Use **a** and **in** for places:
**al mare** (at the seaside)
**in montagna** (in the mountains)
**in campagna** (in the countryside)

**Il sole** is the sun, **il cielo** the sky, **la luce** the light.

**Che ore sono?** asks the time. **Sono le …** for most hours, but **È l'una** (one o'clock), **è mezzogiorno** and **è mezzanotte**, since those are one.

Add **e mezza** (half past), **e un quarto** (a quarter past) or **meno un quarto** (a quarter to): **Sono le tre e mezza.**

**Di mattina**, **di pomeriggio**, **di sera** tell the part of the day.

When you didn't catch something: **Scusi?** (politely) or **Come?**

**Non ho sentito** means I didn't hear.
**Cosa hai detto?** means what did you say?

**Sentito** and **detto** are the past forms of **sentire** (hear) and **dire** (say). **Ho** or **hai** comes before them.

**Lunedì** means this Monday; **il lunedì** means every Monday. **Tutti i giorni** and **ogni giorno** both mean every day.

**Prossimo** (next) and **scorso** (last) agree with the noun: **la settimana prossima**, **la domenica scorsa**.

**Sempre** is always, **spesso** often, **mai** never or ever.

Months take no capital: **gennaio**, **febbraio**, **marzo** … **dicembre**. Say **a gennaio** or **in gennaio** for in January.

Dates use the plain number, **il due maggio**, except for the first: **il primo maggio**.

The seasons are **la primavera**, **l'estate**, **l'autunno**, **l'inverno**.

Words that give you time to think: **Un attimo…** **Vediamo** (let's see).

**Allora**, **dunque** and **quindi** all mean so or then: **Allora, dove vado?**

**Penso di sì** means I think so.

**Venire** is irregular: **vengo**, **vieni**, **viene**. **Uscire** too: **esco** (I go out).

**Possiamo** + a verb makes a suggestion: **Possiamo andare insieme?**
**Andiamo al cinema** means let's go to the cinema.

**Libero** and **occupato** agree: **sei libera domani?**

**Fare** is irregular: **faccio**, **fai**, **fa**. **Fare colazione** is to have breakfast.

Some **-ire** verbs add **-isc-**: **finire**, **finisco**.

**Prima** (before), **poi** (then) and **dopo** (after) put your day in order.

Signs use short words: **Aperto**, **Chiuso**, **Entrata**, **Uscita**, **Vietato** (forbidden).

When a word describes a noun it agrees: **la banca è aperta**, **il negozio è chiuso**.

**Vietato** + a verb forbids something: **vietato nuotare**.

**Partire** (to leave) and **arrivare** (to arrive): **il treno parte**, **il treno arriva**.

On a timetable you read **partenza** (departure), **arrivo** (arrival) and **binario** (platform).

**Un biglietto di andata** is one way; **andata e ritorno** is a return.

To say you're not sure:
**Non sono sicuro** (a man)
**non sono sicura** (a woman)
**Credo di sì** (I think so)
**forse** (maybe)
**probabilmente** (probably)

**Sembra** means it seems, and **davvero?** means really?

Announcements open with **Signore e signori, attenzione.**

**Il treno è in ritardo** means the train is late.
**A causa di** means because of, and **per questo motivo** for this reason.

Instructions to one person you know use the **tu** command: **ascolta**, **guarda**, **rispondi**, **scegli**, **metti** (often the same as the **tu** or **lui** form).

To a class, the **voi** command: **leggete**, **scrivete**.

Forms often use the infinitive instead: **Inserire il nome.**

Words that join: **ma** (but), **o** and **oppure** (or), **se** (if), **senza** (without), **tra** and **fra** (between, or in, for time).

**Di**, **a**, **da**, **in** and **su** join the article:
**di** + **il** is **del**
**in** + **la** is **nella**
**da** + **il** is **dal**

**Del caffè** means some coffee.

The words of a headline: **il governo**, **il presidente**, **lo stato** (**lo** before **s** + consonant), **la politica**, **la guerra** and **la pace**.

**La notizia** is one piece of news; **le notizie** is the news.

Everyday verbs side by side: **metto** (I put), **do** (I give), **guardo** (I look), **aspetto** (I wait), **provo** (I try), **uso** (I use).

**Dare** is irregular: **do**, **dai**, **dà**.

**Riuscire a** + a verb is to manage to: **non riesco a ricordare**.

**Mi piace** for one thing, **mi piacciono** for more than one. **Preferisco** (I prefer) adds **-isc-**.

**Meglio** is better as an adverb (**canta meglio**); **migliore** as an adjective (**il libro migliore**).

**Avere ragione** is to be right, **avere torto** to be wrong.

Italy has **regioni** (regions), each with **province** (provinces) and **comuni** (towns with their own council).

**La gente** (people) takes a singular verb: **la gente è simpatica**.

At the bar: **Un caffè, per favore**, or **Prendo un cornetto**.

**Prendiamo** means we'll have.
**Offro io** means it's my treat; **il bar offre**, the bar offers.
**Basta così** means that's enough.
**A me piace …** puts the stress on **me**.

**Permesso?** asks to get past someone or to come in.
**Mi fa un favore?** asks a favour politely.
**C'è qualcuno?** (is anyone there?)
**nessun problema** (no problem)

**Aiutare** is to help: **mi può aiutare?**

**Ordinare** is to order: **ordino**, **ordini**.

An Italian meal has:
**il primo** (pasta, rice or soup)
**il secondo** (meat or fish)
**il dolce** (dessert)

**Un piatto di pasta** is a plate of pasta: **di** after the amount, as with **un chilo di**.

Directions: **a destra** (on the right), **a sinistra** (on the left), **dritto** (straight on).

Where things are: **davanti a** (in front of), **dietro** (behind), **di fronte a** (opposite), **sotto** (under).

Distance with **a**: **la farmacia è a cento metri**.

**Mi sono perso** (a man) or **mi sono persa** (a woman) means I'm lost; **sono perso** is fine too.

**Gira a destra** means turn right.
**Tornare indietro** is to go back.

**Guidare** is to drive: **guido**.

**Salire** (**salgo**) is to get on, **scendere** (**scendo**) to get off: **salgo sul treno**, **scendo qui**.

**In macchina**, **in tram**, **in treno**, but **a piedi** (on foot).

**Entro** means by, no later than: **entro domani**.

With a family word in the singular, **mio**, **tuo** and **suo** come without the article: **mio padre**, **mia sorella**, **tuo fratello**.

In the plural the article comes back: **i miei genitori**, **i tuoi figli**.

**Sposato** and **sposata** agree.

**La casa ha tre stanze**: **stanza** is any room, **camera** often the bedroom (**camera da letto**).

Words for things at home: **la porta**, **la finestra**, **la sedia**, **il divano**, **l'armadio**.

**Un oggetto** is a thing, **gli oggetti** the things.

**Lavoro in un'azienda**, **lavoro per il comune**: **in** or **per**.

**Il capo** is the boss, **il collega** or **la collega** the colleague. **Lo stipendio** is the salary.

**Avere esperienza** is to have experience.

**Non funziona** means it doesn't work; **manca qualcosa**, something is missing.

**Bisogna** + a verb means one has to: **bisogna aspettare**.

**È grave?** asks if it's serious; **una soluzione** is a solution.

The words on a form: **nome**, **cognome**, **data di nascita**, **luogo di nascita**, **stato civile** (**sposato**, **sposata**), **professione**, **residenza**, **firma**.

Forms use the infinitive for what to do: **Indicare la data**, **Inserire il nome**.

**Dichiaro** means I declare.

Letters and postcards open with **Caro Marco** or **Cara Anna** (**caro** agrees). They end with **Saluti**, **Tanti saluti** or **Un abbraccio**.

**Ti invio** means I'm sending you; **inviare** is to send.

Adjectives in **-e** are the same for both genders: **generale**, **principale**, **attuale**, **regionale**.

Adjectives in **-o** agree: **specifico**, **specifica**; **numeroso**, **numerosa**.

Most adjectives come after the noun: **la strada principale**, **un problema tecnico**.

Verbs of thinking and saying: **considero**, **ritengo** (I consider, I believe), **propongo** (I suggest).

Many are used in the **lui** form: **esiste** (exists), **appare** (appears), **risulta** (turns out), **riguarda** (concerns).

**Ti rende felice?** means does it make you happy?

Everyday verbs in the **lui** form: **offre**, **permette**, **contiene**, **richiede**.

Some are irregular: **ottenere** (**ottengo**), **porre** (**pone**), **proporre** (**propone**).

**Imparare una lingua richiede tempo**: the subject usually comes first.

Words for ideas and everyday things: **il caso** (case), **il senso** (sense), **il valore** (value), **lo scopo** (aim), **la possibilità**, **la proposta**, **l'azione**, **il corpo** (body).

**Prendersi cura di** means to take care of: **Mi prendo cura di Tom**.

Set phrases: **in questo caso**, **in ogni caso**.

**Ciò** means this or that, as a pronoun: **Ciò non ha senso**.

Words of study and culture: **la ricerca** (research), **il programma**, **il livello**, **la prova** (test), **la conoscenza** (knowledge), **la cultura**, **l'autore**, **la serie** (a TV series, the same in the plural).

**Fare una ricerca** is to do some research.

**Il consiglio** is advice (and a council); **l'istituto** and **l'associazione** are places and groups of learning.
